title: A People Confesses: God's Faithfulness and Israel's Failure
summary: Later in the same month the Israelites gather in fasting and sackcloth, separate from foreigners, read the Law, and confess their sins. The Levites lead a long prayer that retells Israel's history from creation and Abraham through the exodus, the wilderness, the conquest, the judges, and the prophets to the exile, praising God's faithfulness and admitting Israel's repeated rebellion. The prayer ends by describing the people as slaves in their own land and announcing that they will make a binding written agreement.
story: Chapter 8 ended with the joy of the Feast of Booths. Two days after that feast closes, on the twenty-fourth of the seventh month, the tone changes to sorrow and confession, the mourning that the leaders had told the people to hold back on the holy day (8:9-11). The prayer that fills most of the chapter is one of the longest in the Bible and one of the fullest summaries of the Old Testament story told by Israel itself. It explains how the community came to be where it is, and it leads directly into chapter 10, where the people put their names to a covenant pledge. The prayer looks back over the whole story so that the people can take their place in it honestly.
historical:
The setting is the autumn of about 445 BC, if the events follow the completion of the wall. Judah was a province of the Persian Empire, paying tribute and governed by officials appointed by the king. The prayer's closing complaint that the people are slaves in their own land (verses 36-37) reflects this situation. Persia's rule had allowed the return and the rebuilding, and Nehemiah himself served the Persian king, yet the prayer is frank that political subjection is a consequence of Israel's sin and that the harvest of the land goes to foreign kings.

The prayer's historical survey reaches from the days of the kings of Assyria (verse 32), who conquered the northern kingdom and destroyed Samaria in 722 BC, down to the present. Behind its middle section stand the books of Exodus through Kings: the calf at Sinai, the victories over Sihon and Og east of the Jordan, the cycle of oppression and rescue in Judges, and the prophets rejected under the monarchy.
cultural:
Fasting, sackcloth (a rough garment of goat or camel hair), and dust on the head were the ordinary signs of mourning and repentance in Israel and the surrounding world. Standing to confess (verses 2-3) was a posture of attention before God. The day was divided into quarters, with about three hours of reading and three of confession and worship, which shows how the pattern of chapter 8, reading followed by response, was being repeated.

The separation from foreigners in verse 2 was a ritual act for this occasion: those of Israelite descent confessed the sins of their own ancestors, a confession that outsiders could not make on their behalf. Confessing the sins of one's fathers alongside one's own was a recognized form of prayer after the exile (compare Daniel 9 and Ezra 9). It expressed solidarity with earlier generations rather than blaming them, and it showed that the people understood their history as one story under one covenant.
literary: After a narrative introduction (verses 1-5a), the prayer (verses 5b-38) moves through Israel's history in stages, and each stage contrasts what God did with how the people responded. God creates and chooses (6-8), rescues from Egypt (9-11), guides and gives the law (12-15); the people rebel, and God forgives (16-21). God gives the land (22-25); the people rebel, and God disciplines and rescues again and again (26-31). The final section (32-38) turns from history to present request. Repeated phrases hold the structure together: “You gave”, “You heard”, and especially the confession of God's compassion (verses 17, 19, 27, 28, 31), set against the refrain that the people stiffened their necks (verses 16, 17, 29). The prayer draws heavily on the language of earlier Scripture, including God's self-description in Exodus 34:6. Most English translations follow the Hebrew in giving the prayer to the Levites; the Greek Septuagint introduces verse 6 with the words that Ezra spoke.

outline.t: A day of fasting, reading, and confession
The Creator who chose Abraham and kept his promise
Exodus, Sinai, and provision in the wilderness
Rebellion in the wilderness and the God who did not forsake them
Rebellion, discipline, and rescue in the land
Confession for the present: slaves in their own land
The decision to make a binding agreement

doctrines.note: The people confess “their sins and the iniquities of their fathers” (verse 2) and declare, “You are just in all that has befallen us” (verse 33). Biblical repentance accepts God's judgment as right and does not excuse itself by blaming earlier generations or circumstances.

The prayer's anchor is God's character: “But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion” (verse 17), language taken from God's own words to Moses in Exodus 34:6. God's faithfulness is the constant in a history of human failure.

God “keeps His gracious covenant” (verse 32) and made a covenant with Abraham that he kept “because You are righteous” (verse 8). The whole history is told as the story of God's faithfulness to his promises, which is why the people can respond with a covenant commitment of their own.

The prayer twice speaks of God's Spirit: “You gave Your good Spirit to instruct them” (verse 20), and the Spirit admonished Israel through the prophets (verse 30). In the Old Testament the Spirit is the presence and power of God guiding and warning his people.

words.note: Rachamim, compassion or mercy. The word is related to the Hebrew for womb and suggests the deep, protective love of a parent. It is the prayer's recurring explanation for why Israel still exists: “in Your great compassion” God did not forsake them (verses 19, 27, 28, 31).

Oreph, the back of the neck. To stiffen the neck is a picture drawn from farm animals that refuse the yoke or the driver's direction. It describes stubborn refusal to be led, and it recurs in the prayer (verses 16, 17, 29) as Israel's characteristic sin.

Chesed, steadfast love, translated here “loving devotion” (verse 17) and “gracious” covenant (verse 32). It is loyal love that keeps its commitments. The prayer depends on it: Israel's hope rests on God's chesed, not on its own record.

Amanah, a firm agreement. The word in verse 38 is related to the root meaning firm or reliable, the same family as amen. It is not the usual word for covenant, but it describes a binding, written commitment, which the people now make in response to God's faithfulness.

christ: The prayer tells Israel's story as a long pattern of God's faithfulness and human failure, ending with the people still in a kind of bondage and waiting. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one in whom that pattern is finally resolved: he is the faithful Israelite who keeps the covenant, and God's compassion is shown decisively in him. Several images in the prayer are taken up by Jesus himself. He calls himself the true bread from heaven, contrasting himself with the manna of the wilderness (John 6:31-35), and Paul speaks of the rock in the wilderness as Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Stephen's speech in Acts 7 retells Israel's history in a similar way, including the rejection of the prophets, and applies it to the rejection of Jesus. The link in each case is the New Testament's reading of the story, which this prayer helped to shape.

hard.q: The prayer says God's ordinances are those “by which a man will live if he practices them”. Does this mean salvation comes by keeping the law?
hard.a:
Verse 29 quotes the principle of Leviticus 18:5, which Ezekiel also repeats (Ezekiel 20:11). In context, the prayer's point is that the law was given for Israel's good, a way of life in the land, and that Israel refused it. Paul later quotes the same principle in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12, contrasting righteousness based on the law with righteousness based on faith, which has led to debate about how the two relate.

Interpreters read this in different ways. Many in the Reformation tradition see Leviticus 18:5 as stating a real principle that no sinner can fulfill, which drives people to seek righteousness as a gift in Christ. Others argue that in Leviticus the promise of life belonged to a people already redeemed by grace from Egypt, so that obedience was the response to salvation, not its cause, and that Paul is contrasting two ways of reading the law rather than two ways of salvation. Nehemiah 9 itself fits either reading: the same prayer that praises the good law also rests all of Israel's hope on God's compassion, not on the people's record.

questions: The prayer tells Israel's history honestly, including its worst moments. What would it look like to tell the story of your own life, or your church, with the same honesty about failure and the same confidence in God's faithfulness?
Verse 17 describes God as “slow to anger and rich in loving devotion.” Where have you seen that patience in your own experience?
The people said, “You are just in all that has befallen us.” When is it right to accept hardship as discipline, and when is suffering not a punishment at all?
